title: Chapter 149: The Most Dangerous Patient
html:
“Room 5 held a man named Xu Tong. He suffered from the Fregoli delusion, which convinced him that everyone around him was the same person in disguise. He lived in a reality entirely of his own making.

“The patient in Room 6 was Han Bao’er, a late-night television host. Her file contains no photograph, but her attending physician wrote a single line at the bottom of her record—How cruel must God be to create a woman this beautiful?

“Han Bao’er stayed for only two and a half months before someone removed her. She suffered from a rare condition called body dysmorphic disorder. She magnified every perceived imperfection and could not tolerate the slightest flaw. During her hospitalization, she once tried to cut off her own fingers because the nails on her two hands were not perfectly symmetrical.

“The name of the patient in Room 7 has been lost. He suffered from Cotard’s syndrome, also known as walking corpse syndrome. He believed himself already dead and told the doctors that his organs had rotted away. He insisted to anyone who would listen that he had seen the true world and that our reality was an illusion.

“Room 8 had a reinforced steel door. Its patient, Xiong Qing, had once been a doctor at the Third Sick Hall. People believed that treating too many tormented minds had broken his own. At thirty, he was diagnosed with hemispatial neglect, a condition that left him unaware of one side of his surroundings. Asked to draw a person, he omitted half the arms and legs. When questioned, he called the result the only perfect human form.

“The condition itself was not severe, but Xiong Qing was a perfectionist. Whenever he saw patients with all their limbs intact, he could not suppress the urge to ‘correct’ them.

“Room 9 held Wu Fei. Even when the hospital closed, he had no definitive diagnosis. Some doctors suspected Asperger’s syndrome because of his extraordinary memory and intelligence. He rarely spoke to anyone—perhaps he considered everyone around him, including his doctors, too stupid to deserve conversation.

“During treatment, he confessed to numerous crimes, several of which had involved the police. Most of his stories proved false, while the genuine crimes had already been solved and their perpetrators convicted. None had any connection to Wu Fei. He had never harmed anyone during his hospitalization, yet the hospital and police still agreed, after extensive discussion, to confine him in Room 9.

“Given the hospital’s system, Room 10 should have contained the most dangerous patient of all, but the records give him no name. In every file, the name field contains only the number ten. The doctors never referred to him by name. Most called him the Devil.

“He suffered from Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, also called juvenile gout. During an episode, he would use anything within reach to mutilate his own face. His perception of reality was profoundly distorted, and he was violently self-destructive. Patient 10 spent most of his time strapped to a bed. Whenever he left it, attendants chained him into a wheelchair.

“People with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome rarely live past twenty, so Patient 10 is probably dead by now.”

As Doctor Gao described the nine patients, Chen Ge wrote down every detail. Reading over his notes sent a chill along his spine. “Do you know what happened to them after they were transferred out of the Third Sick Hall?”

“Only Wang Shenglong, Xu Tong, and Han Bao’er have records from other hospitals. The rest seem to have vanished.”

“Do you have any way to contact those three?” Chen Ge wanted to learn as much as possible before beginning the livestream.

“Most of the phone numbers in the files are no longer in service, so giving them to you would accomplish nothing.” Doctor Gao declined tactfully. “I called this late mainly to warn you that Wang Shenglong may be dangerous. Some psychiatric patients can behave like different people during an episode. Do not provoke him deliberately. If he hurts you, his mental condition may limit his legal responsibility.”

Doctor Gao’s meaning was clear. He had noticed the smooth carpet after Chen Ge’s fall and suspected that Chen Ge had been pushed rather than tripped. This midnight call was his way of warning him about the danger.

“I understand. I’ll be careful.” After a moment’s thought, Chen Ge added, “If you uncover anything else about the Third Sick Hall, please let me know. I’m very interested in that hospital.”

“You certainly have unusual interests. All right, get some rest. I’ll contact you if I discover anything new.”

After the call ended, Chen Ge spread his notes across the table and contemplated the nine patients. Ten rooms, but only nine patients. Why? If the rooms corresponded to danger level, why leave Room 3 empty? Was it always vacant, or had it belonged to a patient who died there?

He did not remember falling asleep. By the time he woke, dawn had arrived and his watch read six. He washed his face, left the Haunted House, mounted his bicycle, and headed for the nearest morning market.

Though the day had barely begun, the market was already bustling. Chen Ge stood out among the middle-aged shoppers. He bought a live rooster first, then stopped at a pork stall and watched the cleaver in the proprietor’s hand.

When the proprietor finally had a free moment, Chen Ge stepped forward. The man, about forty, had noticed him lingering some time ago. “What do you want?”

Voicing the request felt strangely embarrassing. “I want to buy your cleaver.”

“My cleaver?” The man’s expression darkened, as if Chen Ge were mocking him.

“I’m serious.” Chen Ge placed some money on the counter. “Name your price.”

After a lengthy explanation, the man finally understood what kind of cleaver Chen Ge wanted and laughed. “It’s not that I refuse to sell it. These days, slaughterhouses use specialized machines. You’ll have to find an old-fashioned butcher if you want a blade steeped in that much blood.”
